chapter_summary:
Before out-of-order execution became dominant, in-order processors used dynamic scheduling techniques to improve performance. The **scoreboard** is one of the earliest dynamic scheduling algorithms, used in the CDC 6600 supercomputer (1964).

**Scoreboard components:**

The scoreboard tracks the status of instructions, functional units, and registers. It has three main tables:

1. **Instruction Status Table:** Tracks the stage of each instruction (Issue, Read Operands, Execute, Write Result).

2. **Functional Unit Status Table:** Tracks the state of each functional unit. For each unit, it records:
   - Busy: Whether the unit is in use.
   - Operation: The operation being performed.
   - Destination register (Fi): The register that will receive the result.
   - Source registers (Fj, Fk): The registers that hold the operands.
   - Functional units producing the source operands (Qj, Qk): If an operand is being produced by another unit, this records which unit.
   - Ready flags (Rj, Rk): Whether the operands are ready.

3. **Register Result Table:** Tracks which functional unit will write to each register. If a register is not being written by any unit, the entry is empty.

**Scoreboard algorithm:**

An instruction proceeds through four stages:

1. **Issue:** The instruction is issued to a functional unit if:
   - The required functional unit is free.
   - No other instruction is writing to the same destination register (WAW hazard check).
   If the instruction cannot be issued, it is stalled until the conditions are met.

2. **Read Operands:** The instruction reads its operands from the register file when:
   - Both operands are ready (no other instruction is writing to the source registers).
   - The source registers are not waiting to be read by earlier instructions (WAR hazard check for CDC 6600, but not for modern implementations).
   If the operands are not ready, the instruction waits.

3. **Execute:** The functional unit performs the operation. When complete, the functional unit notifies the scoreboard.

4. **Write Result:** The result is written to the register file if:
   - No other instruction is currently reading the old value of the destination register (WAR hazard check).
   If a WAR hazard exists, the write is delayed until the reading instruction completes.

**Limitations of scoreboarding:**

The scoreboard does not use register renaming, so it cannot eliminate WAR and WAW hazards. It must stall instructions to avoid these hazards. This limits the amount of parallelism that can be extracted.

For example, if instruction I1 writes to R1 and instruction I2 (which appears later) also writes to R1, a WAW hazard occurs. The scoreboard must stall I2 until I1 writes its result. In an out-of-order processor with register renaming, both instructions can execute simultaneously because they write to different physical registers.

**Scoreboard vs. Tomasulo:**

| Feature | Scoreboard | Tomasulo's Algorithm |
|---------|------------|----------------------|
| WAR/WAW handling | Stall | Register renaming eliminates hazards |
| Operand availability | Check register file | Wait for result on CDB |
| Functional units | Fixed assignment | Reservation stations, flexible assignment |
| Complexity | Moderate | Higher |
| Performance | Good for its era | Much better for wide issue |

Tomasulo's algorithm (discussed in Module 6) improves upon the scoreboard by using register renaming and reservation stations, eliminating WAR and WAW hazards and allowing more flexible scheduling.

screens.title: In-Order Multiple Issue and Scoreboarding
screens.subtitle: How an early dynamic scheduler tracked instructions, functional units, and registers to extract parallelism in-order

narration.text: In this chapter we explore the scoreboard, an early dynamic scheduling technique used in in-order multiple-issue processors. The scoreboard tracks each instruction’s stage, records which functional unit will produce a result, and records whether source operands are ready. You will learn the scoreboard’s three tables — instruction status, functional unit status, and the register result table — and how they coordinate the four-stage flow: Issue, Read Operands, Execute, and Write Result. We will examine why the scoreboard must stall some instructions to avoid WAR and WAW hazards, and why scoreboarding cannot eliminate these hazards without register renaming. You will also compare scoreboarding to Tomasulo’s algorithm to see how renaming and reservation stations remove certain stalls and improve performance. A hands-on simulation of a small instruction sequence will make the effects concrete: you will read the instruction timelines, identify stalls, and see how dependence chains propagate through the tables. Understanding the scoreboard gives you a clear lens into the trade-offs between hardware complexity and performance when scheduling in-order processors.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Scoreboarding enabled early high-performance processors to exploit instruction-level parallelism while keeping in-order semantics, trading hardware simplicity for occasional stalls due to hazards.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four clear skills. First, you will be able to explain how an in-order multiple-issue processor can dispatch instructions to several functional units while still appearing in-order to the program. This matters because in-order designs gain parallelism without the full cost of out-of-order hardware. Second, you will be able to describe the scoreboard algorithm: how it tracks instruction stage, functional unit state, and which unit will write each register. Knowing the tables and fields helps you read and predict stalls. Third, you will understand the scoreboard’s limitations: because it does not use register renaming it cannot eliminate WAR and WAW hazards, so you will be able to identify situations that force stalls. Finally, you will be able to compare scoreboarding with Tomasulo’s algorithm and explain why renaming and reservation stations reduce stalls. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual link to help you remember when to apply the concept during scheduling analysis.

narration.text: This second objectives slide gives practical cues you can use while reading tables and timelines. For dispatch, habitually check functional unit availability and destination conflicts — ask: is the unit busy and is anyone else going to write this register? For the scoreboard tables, practice scanning three lists: the per-instruction stage, the functional unit rows with Busy, Fi, Fj, Fk, Qj, Qk, Rj, Rk, and the register result mapping that shows which unit will write each register. For hazards, train yourself to spot WAW when two instructions will write the same register, and WAR when a later writer could overwrite a register before an earlier reader uses it. For comparison, use the simple rule: scoreboarding preserves architectural register names and therefore must stall; Tomasulo renames and therefore can proceed. screens.title: What is the Scoreboard?
screens.subtitle: A definition and the role it played in early multiple-issue processors

narration.text: The scoreboard is a dynamic scheduler that coordinates instruction progress in in-order multiple-issue processors. It is not a rename-based out-of-order engine. Instead, it maintains three explicit tables: an instruction status table that records the stage of each instruction; a functional unit status table that shows which unit is busy, which operation it runs, the destination register, the source registers, and whether operands are ready; and a register result table that records which functional unit will write each architectural register. Together these tables let the processor delay only the operations that would violate in-order semantics or cause incorrect reads. A concrete example: if an ADD is issued to an ALU and will later write F1, the register result table marks F1 as pending from that ALU. Another instruction that needs F1 as an operand will check that table or the functional unit’s ready flags and wait if the value is not yet available. A common misconception is to think scoreboarding allows full parallel execution without conflicts; it does not. Because it keeps architectural register names, WAR and WAW hazards force stalls that a renaming scheme would avoid. The core takeaway is that the scoreboard is a tracking and arbitration mechanism that trades hardware simplicity for occasional stalls to preserve program correctness.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A centralized control that tracks instructions, units, and register writers to schedule in-order multiple-issue execution safely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is the Scoreboard?
Definition

Scoreboard as a scheduler

The scoreboard coordinates instruction stages by maintaining centralized tables that represent the state of every instruction, each functional unit, and pending register results. It preserves in-order semantics while allowing some parallel execution when possible.

Concrete example
An ADD that will write F1 marks F1 in the register result table. Any later consumer checks that entry before reading F1.
Common misconception
Scoreboarding is not register renaming. It cannot eliminate WAR/WAW hazards, so some parallelism remains blocked.
Key Takeaway

The scoreboard tracks who will produce each register and enforces safe progression through Issue, Read, Execute, and Write stages.

Instruction Status
  • Issue
  • Read Operands
  • Execute
  • Write Result
Register Result Table
Maps each architectural register to the functional unit that will write it. Empty means no pending writer.
Functional Unit Row
Fields: Busy, Operation, Fi, Fj, Fk, Qj, Qk, Rj, Rk — these connect producer/consumer relationships.
Analogy
Think of the scoreboard as an airport control board assigning gates, tracking which plane is at which gate and which baggage belongs to which flight.

screens.title: Scoreboard Tables: Instruction Status
screens.subtitle: Track an instruction's progress through Issue, Read Operands, Execute, and Write Result

narration.text: The Instruction Status table records the lifecycle stage for each instruction: Issue, Read Operands, Execute, and Write Result. Each row corresponds to a dispatched instruction and is updated as the processor grants resources and operands become available. Practically, this table lets you follow an instruction from the moment it is allocated to a functional unit until its result is committed to the register file. Consider an ADD that issues to an ALU: the table first marks it as Issued. If operands are ready, the table moves it to Read Operands and then to Execute, where the functional unit holds a busy flag. When execution completes, the table records Write Result pending and waits until the scoreboard confirms no WAR hazard exists before committing the write. One useful reading habit is to scan this table in tandem with the functional unit table: a long gap between Execute finish and Write Result indicates a write-to-read conflict elsewhere. That gap is precisely where scoreboarding can force a stall, and it is often the performance-limiting window in in-order multiple-issue designs. Scoreboard Tables: Instruction Status means provides a timeline for each instruction and reveals where stalls occur between execution completion and register writes.. In practical terms, track an instruction's progress through issue, read operands, execute, and write result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Role of Instruction Status
keyIdea.text: Provides a timeline for each instruction and reveals where stalls occur between execution completion and register writes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Instruction Status
Instruction Status Table
Each row tracks an instruction's stage. This table is the departure board for in-order scheduling.
Fields
Instruction ID, Operation, Stage (Issue, Read Operands, Execute, Write Result), cycle timestamps
Reading tip
Compare timestamps to find where an instruction waits: stalled at Issue vs delayed at Write Result indicate different hazards.
Example row
I3: MUL — Issue: cycle 2, Read Operands: cycle 4, Execute: cycles 5-8, Write Result: pending
Key Takeaway

The Instruction Status table is the primary source to spot where hazards turn into stalls across cycles.

screens.title: Functional Unit Status Table
screens.subtitle: Fields that connect producers and consumers: Busy, Operation, Fi, Fj, Fk, Qj, Qk, Rj, Rk

narration.text: The functional unit status table is the scoreboard’s most detailed control surface. For each functional unit it records whether the unit is Busy, the Operation being performed, the Destination register (Fi), source register names (Fj, Fk), which functional units will produce those sources (Qj, Qk), and ready flags (Rj, Rk). Busy tells you whether a unit can accept a new Issue. Fi shows the architectural register to which the result will be written. Fj and Fk are the source registers named in the instruction; if Qj or Qk is set, it means another unit will produce that operand, so the current unit must wait until the producing unit sets Rj or Rk to true. This table is how the scoreboard encodes data dependencies without renaming: producer and consumer units are linked directly by Q fields. A concrete scenario: an earlier ADD is in an ALU producing F1; a later MUL uses F1 as Fj, so MUL's Qj points to the ADD’s unit and Rj is false until ADD completes. That chain of references creates the stalls you will read when walking cycle tables. Understanding these fields is essential to predict when Read Operands can move forward and when execution will begin.

keyIdea.title: Producer–Consumer Links
keyIdea.text: Q and R fields implement direct links from a consumer unit to the producing unit, enabling operand tracking without renaming.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Functional Unit Status
Functional Unit Row
Busy | Operation | Fi | Fj | Fk | Qj | Qk | Rj | Rk
Busy and Operation
Indicate whether the unit can accept a new issue and which opcode it is performing.
Q and R fields
Qj/Qk name the producing unit when an operand is pending; Rj/Rk mark readiness. These are the heart of producer-consumer links.
Example rows
ALU1: Busy=Yes, Op=ADD, Fi=F1, Fj=F2, Fk=F3, Qj=-, Qk=-, Rj=1, Rk=1
MUL1: Busy=Yes, Op=MUL, Fi=F4, Fj=F1, Fk=F5, Qj=ALU1, Qk=-, Rj=0, Rk=1
Key Takeaway

Q and R fields explicitly encode where an operand will come from and whether it is ready, enabling staged reads and safe execution starts.

screens.title: Register Result Table
screens.subtitle: How the scoreboard records which unit will write each architectural register

narration.text: The Register Result Table maps architectural registers to the functional unit that will later write them. This table is crucial because the scoreboard does not rename registers: it uses the architectural names directly. When an instruction is issued and assigned to a functional unit, the scoreboard records that functional unit as the producer for the destination register. Any later instruction consulting that register checks the entry: if the entry points to a functional unit, the operand is not yet in the register file and the consumer must either wait or read when the producing unit signals readiness. A concrete example: an ADD that issues first will mark F1 -> ALU1 in the register result table. If a subsequent instruction needs F1, it will see that ALU1 is the producer and the consumer’s Q field will reference ALU1 until ALU1 sets the corresponding R flag. A common trap is assuming this table allows multiple pending writers to the same register; it does not. If a second instruction also intends to write the same architectural register, the scoreboard will prevent it from being issued to avoid WAW hazards. That conservative policy preserves correctness but limits parallelism compared to renaming designs.

keyIdea.title: No renaming here
keyIdea.text: The register result table ties architectural names to producing units, so multiple writers to the same architectural register force serialization.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Register Result Table
Register Result Table
Maps each architectural register to the functional unit that will write it. Empty if no pending writer.
Concrete behavior
When an instruction issues, the scoreboard sets RegResult[dest] = unit. Later reads check this entry to determine whether to read from the register file or wait for a producing unit.
Performance trade-off
Because the table uses architectural names, it cannot support two concurrent writers to the same register without stalling the later one.
Example snapshot
RegResult: F1 => ALU1; F4 => MUL1; F2 => -
Key Takeaway

Because registers are not renamed, the scoreboard enforces write ordering at the architectural register level, creating WAW-induced stalls.

screens.title: Scoreboard Algorithm Stages
screens.subtitle: Issue → Read Operands → Execute → Write Result explained step-by-step

narration.text: The scoreboard advances instructions through four explicit stages. Issue: the scoreboard assigns the instruction to a compatible free functional unit if no WAW conflict exists on the destination register. If either condition fails, the instruction is stalled at Issue. Read Operands: the instruction reads operands when both operands are ready and when the scoreboard verifies no earlier instruction will read the old value (a WAR concern in some implementations). If operands are produced by other units, the instruction waits until those units set ready flags. Execute: once operands are read, the functional unit executes the operation for its latency period, holding the Busy flag. When execution finishes, the unit notifies the scoreboard. Write Result: before the scoreboard allows the write to the register file, it checks for WAR hazards: if a younger instruction still needs to read the old value, the write is delayed. Using the airport analogy, Issue is assigning a gate, Read Operands is passenger boarding, Execute is taxiing, and Write Result is takeoff — but if another plane needs the gate’s passengers first, takeoff waits. The key point is that each stage enforces correctness constraints that can create waits even when a functional unit is idle elsewhere.

keyIdea.title: Four stages enforce correctness
keyIdea.text: Each stage includes checks that preserve in-order semantics; those checks are the source of stalls in scoreboarding.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Algorithm Stages
Process Flow

Issue → Read Operands → Execute → Write Result

Issue
Check unit free and WAW. Stall if conflict.
Read Operands
Wait until operands ready; check WAR when relevant.
Execute
Functional unit runs for its latency and then signals completion.
Write Result
Check WAR before writing to avoid overwriting a value needed by earlier readers.
Concrete example
ADD issues to ALU, operands ready → moves to Execute for two cycles → on completion the scoreboard may still delay Write Result if a previous instruction must read the old destination.
Misconception
Do not assume Write Result happens immediately after Execute. Scoreboard may delay for WAR checks even after execution completes.

screens.title: Issuing Instructions and WAW Checks
screens.subtitle: When the scoreboard allows an instruction to be assigned a functional unit

narration.text: Issuing is the first decision point in the scoreboard. For an instruction to issue it must find a compatible free functional unit and must not create a WAW hazard on the destination register. The scoreboard enforces a simple conservative rule: if any earlier instruction will write the same architectural register, the new instruction cannot issue. This prevents two pending writers to one register, avoiding ambiguity in which value is the correct architectural state. A concrete example: if I1 is scheduled to write F1 and I2 later also writes F1, the scoreboard will hold off issuing I2 until I1’s write completes and the register result table is cleared. This prevents a potential WAW hazard. The cost is serialization: the pipeline cannot overlap certain writes even when functional units could physically run both operations. A common mistake is assuming issue only checks unit availability; forgetting the WAW rule leads to incorrect expectations about parallelism. The practical reading tip is to check both the functional unit Busy bits and the register result table before predicting whether an instruction will issue in a given cycle.

keyIdea.title: Issue decision
keyIdea.text: Issue requires both unit availability and no pending writer to the same destination to avoid WAW hazards.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Issue Stage
Issue Checks
1) Functional unit free. 2) No WAW on destination. Both must hold to issue.
Example
I1 writes F1 and is pending. I2 writes F1 later: scoreboard stalls I2 at Issue until I1 completes its write.
Misconception
Issue checks both unit availability and destination conflicts. Missing either leads to wrong schedules.
Reading tip
Scan the register result table first for the destination, then check the target unit’s Busy bit to estimate issue timing.
Key Takeaway

WAW checks at Issue serialize writes to the same architectural register, limiting parallelism compared to rename-based designs.

screens.title: Reading Operands and WAR Hazards
screens.subtitle: When consumers are allowed to read architectural registers

narration.text: The Read Operands stage ensures that an instruction reads correct operand values. An instruction may read operands from the register file only when both operands are ready — that is, no earlier instruction is going to write them — or when the scoreboard has recorded a producing unit and that unit has signaled readiness. The scoreboard also considers WAR hazards: if a later instruction might write a register before an earlier instruction reads it, incorrect values would result. For CDC 6600-style scoreboarding, the system checks that no instruction will write a source register while the reader needs the old value. If such a write is pending, the reader will delay reading. A practical example: I1 reads F2 and F3; I2, after I1 in program order, writes F2. If I2 were allowed to write F2 before I1 reads it, I1 would get the wrong value. Scoreboarding avoids this by serializing the actions. A common pitfall is conflating operand readiness with unit availability — operands may be ready but reads are still held because of pending writes that would create WAR hazards. Reading operand readiness correctly is essential to predict when an instruction can start execution.

keyIdea.title: Safe operand reads
keyIdea.text: Operands must be ready and not subject to pending writes that would create WAR hazards before a read can proceed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Read Operands
Read rules
An instruction reads when operands are ready and no WAR hazard will give it the wrong value.
Example
I1 needs F2; I2 (younger) will write F2. Scoreboard prevents I2’s write from happening before I1 reads.
Fields in play
Rj/Rk readiness flags from the producing unit and RegResult table entries determine whether a value is available to read.
Common pitfall

Ready operands do not always mean immediate read — WAR checks can still delay the read to preserve correct values.

screens.title: Execute and Write Result — Completion and WAR checks
screens.subtitle: How execution completes and why writes may be delayed

narration.text: Execution is the stage where the functional unit performs the operation for its latency. When a functional unit finishes, it signals the scoreboard. However, finishing execution does not automatically update the register file. Before the scoreboard allows a Write Result, it must ensure that writing the new value will not violate WAR hazards — that is, no earlier instruction still needs to read the old value. If a WAR hazard exists, the write is deferred even though the execution is complete and the unit is idle, leading to a window where the unit is finished but the architectural state cannot yet be updated. A concrete scenario: a division finishes producing a destination value, but an earlier instruction that reads the old destination has not yet performed its read; the scoreboard holds the write until the read completes. This delay preserves correctness but can reduce parallelism because the register remains occupied in the register result table and later writers are blocked by WAW checks. The important conceptual point is that execution completion and architectural commit are separated by a safety check that causes stalls in scoreboarding systems.

keyIdea.title: Separate completion and commit
keyIdea.text: Execution can finish before the result is written; WAR checks can delay register updates and thus block subsequent writers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Execute & Write Result
Execution
Functional units run for their latency. On completion they notify the scoreboard.
Write Result gating
Before writing, the scoreboard verifies no earlier reader needs the old value, and only then commits to the register file.
Key Takeaway

Execution completion does not imply immediate architectural update; WAR checks can create a commit delay that limits parallelism.

screens.title: Hazards Scoreboarding Cannot Eliminate
screens.subtitle: Why WAR and WAW require stalls without register renaming

narration.text: Scoreboarding cannot eliminate WAR and WAW hazards because it uses architectural register names and does not rename registers to separate logical writers. WAW occurs when two instructions will write the same architectural register: the scoreboard prevents the later writer from issuing until the earlier writer completes its write. This preserves the architectural write order but serializes writes that renaming could make independent. WAR occurs when a later instruction would write a register while an earlier instruction still needs to read the old value. The scoreboard delays the write until the earlier read completes. Together these constraints ensure correctness but reduce available parallelism. A concrete contrast: two writes to the same destination in a scoreboard design must be sequenced, but in a rename-based design the writes can map to different physical registers, allowing both to proceed concurrently. The practical implication is that while scoreboarding adds useful dynamic scheduling to in-order cores, it cannot match the parallelism of renaming-based out-of-order designs. Understanding these limits clarifies why Tomasulo and later rename-based designs became the standard for wide-issue high-performance processors. Hazards Scoreboarding Cannot Eliminate means war and waw hazards force serialization in scoreboarding; register renaming is required to remove those specific stalls.. In practical terms, why war and waw require stalls without register renaming. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: No renaming ⇒ more stalls
keyIdea.text: WAR and WAW hazards force serialization in scoreboarding; register renaming is required to remove those specific stalls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Hazards
WAR and WAW
WAW
Two writers to same architectural register. Scoreboard stalls later writer at Issue to preserve write order.
WAR
A later writer could overwrite a value before an earlier reader reads it. Scoreboard delays writes until reads finish.
Example contrast
With renaming, WAW disappears because each writer gets a distinct physical register. With scoreboarding, the writers must serialize.
Key Takeaway

Scoreboarding enforces correct ordering at the cost of stalls; register renaming is the mechanism that removes these particular constraints.

screens.title: Simulate a Small Scoreboard Sequence
screens.subtitle: Step through cycles for a two-unit processor using a concrete instruction list

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on sequence provided in the chapter. We simulate a processor with two functional units: one ALU and one multiplier. The instruction sequence is: ADD F1, F2, F3 (ALU, 2 cycles); MUL F4, F1, F5 (MUL, 4 cycles, depends on ADD); SUB F6, F2, F3 (ALU, 2 cycles, independent); DIV F7, F4, F6 (MUL, 6 cycles, depends on MUL and SUB). Begin by issuing ADD to the ALU if it is free and no WAW exists on F1 — it issues immediately and marks RegResult[F1] = ALU. MUL cannot issue until it finds a multiplier free and until the scoreboard allows it with respect to WAW on F4; it also needs F1 as an operand, so its Qj will point to the ALU and Rj will be false until ADD completes. SUB can issue concurrently on the ALU only when the ALU is free and no WAW on F6 — but since ADD uses the ALU, SUB must wait for ALU availability or be issued later depending on functional unit counts. As cycles progress, update the Instruction Status table with timestamps for Issue, Read, Execute intervals, and Write Result. Watch for stalls: MUL waits on ADD’s result, and DIV waits on both MUL and SUB. Comparing this schedule to a simple in-order pipeline without scoreboarding will show reduced interlocks for independent instructions but added stalls where WAR/WAW checks force delays. Running the simulation cycle-by-cycle will help you identify the exact cycles where Q and R fields change and when RegResult entries are cleared.

keyIdea.title: Simulation goal
keyIdea.text: Step the scoreboard tables each cycle to observe how Q/R fields and RegResult entries create stalls and propagate dependencies.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Simulation
Instruction Sequence
ADD F1, F2, F3     # ALU, 2 cycles
MUL F4, F1, F5     # MUL, 4 cycles, depends on ADD
SUB F6, F2, F3     # ALU, 2 cycles, independent
DIV F7, F4, F6     # MUL, 6 cycles, depends on MUL and SUB
Simulation steps
For each cycle: update Issue, check RegResult and unit Busy, set Q/R, advance Execute latencies, and gate Write Result by WAR checks.
What to track
  • Instruction Status rows with stage timestamps
  • Functional Unit rows showing Qj/Qk and Rj/Rk
  • Register Result mapping to identify pending writers
Key Takeaway

Cycle-by-cycle bookkeeping reveals precisely where dependencies create stalls and how they propagate through Q/R and RegResult entries.

narration.text: Summarizing the chapter, keep three compact ideas in mind. First, the scoreboard uses three tables — instruction status, functional unit status, and register result — to track every instruction and resource without renaming. Second, the algorithm progresses instructions through Issue, Read Operands, Execute, and Write Result, applying checks at each stage that preserve in-order semantics but can cause stalls for WAR and WAW hazards. Third, the fundamental limitation is the lack of register renaming: WAW and WAR persist and force serialization of certain operations. Comparing scoreboarding with Tomasulo clarifies the trade-off: scoreboarding is simpler in hardware but offers less parallelism, while Tomasulo’s renaming and reservation stations reduce stalls at the cost of added complexity. Remember the airport analogy: gates are functional units, the departure board is instruction status, and baggage tags are register results. That visual helps you reason about when assignments and writes must wait.

keyIdea.title: Bottom line
keyIdea.text: Scoreboarding is a simple dynamic scheduler that preserved correctness for in-order multiple-issue processors but cannot eliminate hazards without renaming.

Three tables
Instruction status, functional unit status, and register result table coordinate scheduling.
Four stages
Issue, Read Operands, Execute, Write Result — each enforces checks that ensure correctness.
Hazard limits
No renaming means WAR and WAW require stalls; this is the scoreboard’s main limitation.
Summary Takeaway

Scoreboarding was a practical early dynamic scheduler: simpler hardware, correct in-order execution, and limited by name-based hazards that later renaming schemes solved.
